tagline: A former byway network connects parish towns and ancient earthworks
intro: Bienville Trace was a Louisiana state scenic byway network. FHWA’s retained description emphasizes public buildings, museums and archaeology across northern Louisiana. On the US 80 corridor, Louisiana’s tourism office describes farms and forested landscapes between Ruston and the Mississippi state line.

Louisiana’s Act 206 of 2011 deleted the Bienville Trace I and II designations and established the Dixie Overland and Boom or Bust byways. Part of the former US 80 route is now promoted as Historic US 80.

Bastrop’s historic downtown holds celebrations and concerts at its restored 1914 courthouse and Rose Theater. Sterlington is in northern Ouachita Parish near Union Parish. On the US 80 branch, the tourism office’s eastward account runs from Ruston to Monroe and West Monroe, then the Poverty Point excursion near Delhi, and on to Tallulah. The former network included an LA 577 extension to Poverty Point, where earthen ridges overlook the Mississippi floodplain.

moments.title: Bastrop’s courthouse
moments.text: The Morehouse Parish Courthouse was built in 1914 in the Beaux Arts style. Its beige brick walls rise above a raised basement beneath a four-stage dome. Small wings were added in 1935; larger additions doubled the building’s size in 1966, though the central block remains prominent. The copper dome received a complete copper replacement in 2023–2024.

moments.title: Sterlington
moments.text: Sterlington lies in northern Ouachita Parish near the Union Parish boundary. Its population at the 2020 census was 1,980.

moments.title: Poverty Point
moments.text: Poverty Point’s builders raised concentric earthen ridges and mounds above the Mississippi River floodplain. Louisiana State Parks dates the site to 1700–1100 BC. Six C-shaped rows form the central construction, divided by at least four aisles. Stone tools connect the site to distant sources in the Ouachita and Ozark Mountains and the Ohio and Tennessee valleys. Soapstone vessels used material from the Appalachian foothills of Alabama and Georgia.
